item.title: 🔵 Governing the agent workforce: New data on the next frontier of AI risk
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

In the fast-paced world of agentic AI, building agents and defending ROI is yesterday’s news. Today, the more pressing challenge is managing and governing the exploding workforce of agents to mitigate growing enterprise risk.

The problem intensifies as AI agents move from advisory to more active roles. According to a survey of 200 IT and AI decision makers conducted by Foundry and Rubrik, most agents are allowed to act with full (26%) or limited (35%) autonomy.

With access to enterprise systems and authority to execute end-to-end tasks, governance, guardrails, and compliance have become key obstacles to AI agent implementation. This was cited by 42% of survey respondents, along with AI agent management, at 18%. Almost one quarter of respondents (24%) cited security and governance as the biggest barrier to their ability to scale agents, even over technical complexities (17%) and lack of proven ROI (14%).

A single threat actor was seen posing as approximately 32 AI bots, while probing organizations across multiple industries. Sought files included those used to store passwords, API keys, and cloud credentials.

item.title: 🔴 The moat is dry – Part 1: Why the old security model failed
item.description:

In June 2017, a piece of malware called NotPetya got into Merck & Co. without climbing a single wall. It arrived through a backdoor in accounting software supplied by a Ukrainian vendor, the kind of trusted, routine traffic every perimeter is built to let through. It spread to some 40,000 of the drugmaker’s computers, and Merck put the damage at more than $1.4 billion.

Then several of Merck’s insurers argued they owed nothing, because the attack was attributed to Russian military intelligence and their policies excluded acts of war. The fight ended in a confidential settlement in January 2024.

item.title: 🟠 The auditor’s dilemma: Solving the explainability problem in public sector AI
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

In public governance and highly regulated enterprise landscapes, automated decisions demand verifiable accountability. As AI systems transition from internal productivity tools to customer-facing or citizen-impacting utility systems, public sector CIOs and corporate compliance officers face extreme legal and reputational exposure. Black-box models that process data mysteriously and generate unverified outputs are no longer acceptable under frameworks like the EU AI Act. Organizations must be prepared to audit the entire lifecycle of their models.

The core issue for compliance officers is verification. When an AI pipeline assists in determining creditworthiness, analyzing patient diagnostics, or managing civic resource distribution, the underlying software must be auditable from end to end. This requires detailed logging mechanisms that track exactly which verified data sets were used for training, how weights were adjusted, and how localized inference parameters were executed at the moment of decision-making.

item.title: 🟠 Your AI agent learned a better way. Who approved the change?
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Imagine a support team working through complaints after a service outage. Its refund policy normally requires an eligibility review. For this incident, an authorized manager approves an exception: customers on the verified outage list may receive up to $100 without individual review, through Friday.

An agent processes those cases successfully. Later, the system consolidates those case histories into a reusable memory: small, immediate refunds resolve service complaints quickly. The summary preserves the outcome but loses the outage restriction and expiration date.

The following week, the agent retrieves that guidance for a similar complaint from a customer who was not affected by the outage. It issues a refund without review. The payment service checks the agent’s credentials and the dollar limit, but does not check whether the customer qualifies for an active exception.

No attacker is needed in this hypothetical. The case may close faster, yet the agent has begun applying a temporary exception beyond its authorized scope.

item.description:

AI and hybrid work have written new rules for matching a device to a role. Equipping the workforce by persona was once a straightforward exercise: the org chart supplied the groups, a stereotype supplied the requirements, and the model held because most people worked roughly the same way. That no longer holds. AI keeps redrawing what roles need, and hybrid work has scattered where they need it. Together, those two shifts have changed the inputs persona building runs on.

The inputs changed, and the principle held. Smart device fleets still get provisioned by sorting employees into representative types and equipping each accordingly. The older build — a role, a department, a rough sketch — came from a workplace that has since changed shape. item.description:

A vulnerability in Google’s Brotli compression library could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code in applications that use an affected Brotli decoder to process compressed data.

Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, the high-severity flaw was first flagged in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The issue stems from an out-of-bounds write that can corrupt process memory, potentially leading to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or denial of service (DoS).

The Node.js project disclosed the vulnerability on October 21, 2026, alongside security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines. The exposure, however, extended beyond Node.js, forcing Microsoft to release out-of-band security updates for.NET on October 25 to address the same CVE in its Brotli decompression implementation.

AI fluency has long mattered to Sambit Dutta. When he joined global chemical manufacturer Hexion this year as SVP of AI transformation, his strategy included bringing “AI to the masses, where the people can not only just consume AI, but also become what we call builders.”

Dutta has made citizen AI a cornerstone of Hexion’s IT strategy because he believes that when the creativity and domain expertise of employees is centralized and funneled through a business analyst or developer, “there are always things lost in translation.” Further, “there’s a queuing process where that request ultimately gets queued, and then based on dollars and other priorities, never gets executed,” he adds.

Dutta also believes that innovation unleashed at the grassroots level is how enterprises achieve true transformation. And it facilitates change management because people become more receptive to absorbing technology at that level, he says.
